archetype.name: Bell Cow (three-down)
archetype.definition: Robinson is Atlanta's feature back on every down. He takes two-thirds of the team's carries and every goal-line attempt, and he has a long history as a high-volume receiver, though that part of the job has been muted this season.

report.headline: One monster night inflates the line; the workload and creative running are real.
report.take:
Robinson is the engine of an offense that has had nothing else working. Atlanta ranks 32nd in offensive EPA and 32nd in passing EPA, but 5th in rushing EPA. It has started three different quarterbacks in three weeks (Rush, Tagovailoa, Penix) and passes 9.5 points less than situation predicts in neutral states, 30th in the league. Robinson carries 66% of the team's rushes and all five of its goal-line carries. That role is why he leads all backs in scrimmage yards per game and ranks third in PPR scoring despite a broken passing game around him.

The season-level efficiency comes almost entirely from one game. His +0.98 rush yards over expected per attempt looks like a career best. But he was below expected in Weeks 1 and 2 (-7.6 and -5.1 total RYOE against Pittsburgh and Carolina), then ran for +77.5 over expected on 29 carries in the 35-14 win at Green Bay. Green Bay's defense now ranks 27th, and that game also produced both of his rushing touchdowns. Take Week 3 out and he is a 4.3-yards-per-carry back on 37 carries. The career line tempers both readings. His RYOE per attempt has climbed every year (0.39, 0.68, 0.88), so a true level in the high-0.8s is believable. Weeks 1 and 2 looked more like an offense with no passing threat than a decline in the runner.

The receiving numbers say more about the quarterbacks than about him. His -0.336 EPA per target ranks 41st of 49. But 14 of his 16 targets came from Cooper Rush, at -0.475 per target, and 12 were thrown behind the line. This is a back who posted 820 receiving yards and +0.258 EPA per target (10th) last season. He is still gaining 2.49 yards after the catch over expectation. The 10-target Week 1 was a checkdown-heavy game plan with Rush. Since then he has six targets in two games, including two in a blowout win under Penix. Whether Penix restores his 2025-style passing-game role is the biggest open question in his profile.

The running itself has a shape. Outside runs have been dangerous: 13 carries off the two ends average well over 10 yards. Inside work has bogged down: 2.93 yards per carry and -0.224 EPA on middle runs, and a 50% stuff rate on four short-yardage tries. Those are small samples. Still, the pattern fits a back whose value comes from creating in space, not from moving piles.

strengths.title: Creating yards beyond the blocking
strengths.body: His rush yards over expected per attempt has risen in every season of his career, and this year's figure sits on top of that trend. The 2026 number leans heavily on the Green Bay game, but three prior seasons of steady growth make a high-0.8s baseline credible. That kind of creation holds up regardless of who is at quarterback.

strengths.title: Locked-in, run-centric workload
strengths.body: He gets two-thirds of the team carries and 100% of the goal-line work, on an offense that leans on the run harder than almost anyone in neutral situations. A strong run defense keeps games close enough for that plan to hold. The role is the most stable thing about his outlook, and it makes him first in scrimmage yards per game.

strengths.title: Explosive on the perimeter
strengths.body: Runs off right end have succeeded 87.5% of the time, and half of them went for explosive gains. Left-end runs average 13.6 yards. The samples are small (8 and 5 carries), but they match his reputation as a back who wins with acceleration once he reaches the edge. Expect the effect to shrink from these levels but to stay real.

concerns.title: Receiving value lost to QB churn
concerns.body: His per-target EPA is near the bottom of the position. Almost all of that came on Cooper Rush's targets, which were mostly behind-the-line checkdowns. Last season he was a top-10 receiving back by EPA, so this is a product of the offense, not a flaw in his skill set. It only persists if the quarterback situation stays this bad or his target volume stays at the 2-4 per game of Weeks 2-3.

concerns.title: Stalls inside and on short yardage
concerns.body: Middle runs have lost EPA at under 3 yards a carry. His third-down and short-yardage carries have been net negative, with half of the short-yardage tries stuffed. Each sample is tiny (15, 6 and 4 plays). It reads more as a sign of how defenses have played him than as a settled weakness. It does cap his touchdown floor somewhat, even with the goal-line role.

concerns.title: Fumbles with lucky recoveries
concerns.body: He has put the ball on the ground twice but lost neither, which is why he ranks first in fumbles lost. He has had three-fumble seasons twice before. Recovery luck tends to even out, so a lost fumble is a realistic risk for anyone treating his ball security as clean.

trend.note: He scored 31.3, then 11.1, then 35.3 PPR points. Week 1 was built on 10 checkdown targets, Week 2 was a 3-34 blowout in which he played 51% of snaps, and Week 3 was a 194-yard rushing game against a soft defense. The scoring path follows game script and quarterback more than any change in him.

nextGame.headline: Depleted, leaky Saints front sets up a big workload day
nextGame.body:
New Orleans is close to the ideal opponent for his profile. The Saints rank 25th in rush defense EPA, 31st in defensive success rate and 29th in explosive run rate allowed. They give running backs 152 yards a game, 31st, and 1.33 touchdowns, 28th. A defense that leaks explosive runs is exactly what a back who wins on the perimeter wants to see. The 47.5 total is the highest Atlanta has played to this season, and the 1.5-point spread points to a close game. That favors the run-first plan holding for four quarters rather than being abandoned.

Availability tilts the matchup further. The Saints are without linebacker Kaden Elliss (a 100%-snap starter), edge Carl Granderson (65%), and rotation pieces Anfernee Jennings and Christen Miller, which thins the front seven he has to beat. On Atlanta's side, Cooper Rush is inactive and Jack Strand is out, which points to Penix starting again. In their only game together, Penix's two targets to Robinson were productive. The worry is left tackle Jake Matthews (100% of snaps): the latest report has him downgraded to out during the Saints game with a groin injury. Left-tackle runs have been his steadiest interior-adjacent lane, with no stuffs on 15 carries, so losing Matthews could push the run game right and toward the edges.

keyMatchups.title: Saints' explosive-run problem
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans allows explosive runs at one of the highest rates in the league, and it is missing its every-down linebacker and a starting edge. That matches Robinson's outside-run, big-play profile and makes a repeat of the Green Bay-style ceiling plausible.

keyMatchups.title: Left side without Matthews
keyMatchups.body: Matthews has played every snap this season, and runs behind left tackle have avoided stuffs entirely. If he is out for most of the game, expect more right-side and edge runs. His right-end runs have been his most efficient so far, which softens the blow.

keyMatchups.title: Goal-line monopoly vs. soft red zone
keyMatchups.body: He has taken every Falcons goal-line carry and converted two of five. He faces a defense allowing well over a touchdown a game to backs. Scoring opportunities near the line should go to him.

nextGame.watch: Watch his target count with Penix under center. A return to 4-6 looks a game would signal the 2025 receiving role is back, which matters more to his weekly floor than the rushing matchup.

restOfSeason.body:
The role is the sustainable part. Two-thirds of the carries, all the goal-line work and a coaching staff that runs well above expectation give him a high weekly floor of touches. His efficiency should settle closer to his 2025 level (around 5.1 yards per carry and RYOE in the high 0.8s) than to the Green Bay spike. The 194-yard game came against a bottom-six defense in a game script that will not repeat every week.

The upside is in the passing game. He has drawn 70-100+ targets in each of his three seasons, and his current receiving EPA is mostly a Cooper Rush artifact. If Penix settles in, his receiving yards and efficiency should climb back toward last year's form. If the offense keeps cycling quarterbacks, he becomes a heavy-volume runner with checkdown catches. The two fumbles without a loss are luck that likely evens out.
swingFactors: Penix's hold on the starting job

bets.reason: He has 100% of Atlanta's goal-line carries. The Saints allow 1.33 running back touchdowns per game (28th) and are missing two starting front-seven players.
The Saints rank 29th in explosive runs allowed and 31st in RB yards allowed, and a close spread should keep the run plan intact. Matthews' injury and the Week 3 skew of his average keep this a lean.
Atlanta's defense (8th in EPA, 1st against the run) faces a Saints offense without Etienne and Fant, with Kamara questionable. Atlanta's own offense meets a defense ranked 26th in EPA.

confidence.note: Three games, three QBs, one outlier game; role and career history are stable anchors.
